title: AI for the bones and POC, then "go legit"?
author: packetpupper
selftext:
Just a general question to this group.

Life long gamer, I never got into game dev due to the time sink factor and coding barrier. I'm actually a developer as my day job, but more focused on data engineering/sql. I've written basic crud apps in C# but nothing like what I see what I open an unreal/unity tutorial.

Despite that, I do have skills in drawing, 3d modeling, dialogue writing, and music composition, most of the things that people tend to think of as stuff people see. So now with AI tools I feel like my game dev dreams are back on the table with the time/skills I do have. 

My goal is to eventually ship a game to steam, and one that doesn't have to carry the AI label. Mainly because If I pour a bunch of my own self-produced music/art/writing etc into a game, I don't want to take the reputation/engagement. I have several games already i've vibecoded that I think are pretty cool but I'm planning to use them as POCs and then replace all of the AI-generated assets I can with my home made assets.

Is this a path some legit developers are doing, or am I setting myself up to try and go legit with a game, only to get canceled because someone finds some AI artifact I missed.

I'm thinking some of the blockers I might have will be

\- Animation and physics, I have no skills in this. But I'm not against using canned animations like how unreal have blueprints, I just dont necessarily want ai generated animations to get the dread AI label.

\- Gameplay mechanics. If I use AI to help balance say, the card stats of my cards in a card game, is that going to get be AI labeled?

\- Anything else I'm missing?

I don't mean any disrespect to full AI game devs, quite the opposite, as I will be doing a lot of that myself. I just have this personal goal to ship a game where my friends, family, etc who hate AI will actually want to play it and view it as my art, instead of giving credit to AI. Any thoughts/tips to achieve this?

comments.author: MistakeForsaken6653
comments.body: General rule of thumb in my experience anything you can see or hear should not be ai generated or you'll get backlash, code is fine.  Only issue is if you have the ai do all code and you are just blindly copying and pasting it will become a huge mess as the project grows.  It's best you define the systems and how they will interact with each other and use the to generate boilerplate code.  Seems like you can handel the see and hear without the ai which is good.

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
Animation, IMO, pay for the human animators for now. I don’t like what I’m seeing from AI models in terms of quality out / effort in. 

Worry less about the AI label, I think. I mean, who am I to tell you how much to worry about the AI label? Your game will probably succeed or fail and the “reputation” is the opinions of some random people you don’t know.

comments.author: Seerix
comments.body:
In my, admittedly limited, experience people don't seem to actually care if you are straight up about what exactly you used AI for. The mods I've posted on steam workshop have disclaimers that describe what I used AI for and how. Notably, I don't use it to write any human facing text or readmes. That squicks me out tbh.

As far as animations go, depending on your aesthetics/style it might be easier than you think. I'm doing pixel art stylized sprites that are actually 3d models rendered as sprites. You lose some finer detail (which can work in your favor depending on the rest of the game) but the animations are so much easier. And consistent! I've read some people having really good results by giving a video model the object to animate and telling it to make a video of whatever animation you want, then feed that video into codex/claude. Physics... use an existing engine to handle it. I wouldn't try to write my own phsyics solution from scratch unless you really need something specific

comments.author: DreamBigGamesReddit
comments.body: I would recommend using AI as much as you can, and when limitations like usage and ability occur, switch to manual. That workflow should keep you constantly moving forward with speed and a good understanding of your core systems.

comments.author: darkoblivion000
comments.body:
Hi, I’m in a similar spot as you actually. Software engineer by trade, never considered game dev before. I don’t have good drawing / 3d modeling skills but I do plan to write all my dialogue and music.

I have been using AI to build all the core infrastructure and architecture of the game. For visuals i have been purchasing asset packs from the unity store that fit my aesthetic. There have been some megapacks that economically really help get almost all the assets i need. Then im using AI to modify those assets to fit my visual theme. I think i do have to disclose that since AI was at least partially involved in the process

Gameplay mechanics, balancing, calculations, engines, being built or modified with AI do not have to be disclosed.

My biggest struggle right now is with npc profile pictures and renders. With the number of characters I want in my game story, hiring an artist for all those profiles would be extremely cost prohibitive and time consuming. For myself to draw them would… I think degrade the quality of my output and also be extremely time consuming. So I’m a little bit between a rock and a hard place.

Music I’m panning to compose myself with some tracks from c0 if I find suitable ones I like.

I don’t know if I’m right, but ultimately the players will care most about the most artistic elements - music and flat out art. And whether it is all polished and feels thematic and has good gameplay. I think if the game is polished and appealing enough it will outweighs the pieces that are AI labeled (as long as it feels like you are making an effort)
